provider_readback.text:
A fish that spits its answer: can archerfish tell human faces apart?

In two laboratory experiments, separate groups of four Toxotes chatareus learned which face image earned food and which to avoid. During testing, the familiar unrewarded face was paired with one new face at a time, drawn from a pool of 44 images in the first experiment. The fish discriminated above chance.

Four different fish also succeeded with 18 novel faces after colour, mean brightness and the outer head outline were standardized. Only TWO faces appeared per trial. The results show learned image discrimination; they do not demonstrate that fish recognise their owners or use the same cues as humans.

TT-008 | Newport, Wallis, Reshitnyk & Siebeck (2016), Scientific Reports 6:27523. DOI: 10.1038/srep27523
Paper, methods, limitations and full credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-008.html

Archerfish reference photograph: Reichenthal, Ben-Tov & Segev (2018), Front. Neural Circuits 12:18, Fig.1A, CC BY 4.0, cropped; from a separate study (10.3389/fncir.2018.00018). Original conceptual task illustrations, not actual face-test footage or stimuli. Synthetic narration; official Toxic Tales logo.
